los.title: Charting Champions
los.summary: Turn numbers into pictures with Python. Create a medal chart, load a CSV file, and investigate what charts can—and cannot—tell us.
los.contentMd:
# Charting Champions

Turn numbers into pictures with Python. Create a medal chart, load a CSV file, and investigate what charts can—and cannot—tell us.

![A robot celebrates with a gold medal.](img/banner.png)

## Your challenge

By the end you will be able to:

- Store a name and a number in a Python list.
- Use indexes to retrieve values.
- Create a bar chart with Pygal.
- Read rows from a CSV file using a loop.
- Convert text into numbers and compare charts critically.

Allow 60–75 minutes. Work individually or in pairs. You will use Thonny on the lab computer.

The medal counts are a historical teaching sample. The later population and wealth investigation uses fictional countries.

# Charting Champions

![A robot celebrates with a gold medal.](img/banner.png)

## Your challenge

By the end you will be able to:

- Store a name and a number in a Python list.
- Use indexes to retrieve values.
- Create a bar chart with Pygal.
- Read rows from a CSV file using a loop.
- Convert text into numbers and compare charts critically.

Allow 60–75 minutes. Work individually or in pairs. You will use Thonny on the lab computer.

The medal counts are a historical teaching sample. The later population and wealth investigation uses fictional countries.

los.title: Get ready in Thonny
los.contentMd:
# Get ready in Thonny

1. [Download the starter files](archives/charting-champions-starter.zip). In File Explorer, right-click the ZIP, choose **Extract All** and open the extracted folder. Keep `main.py` and the four CSV files together.
2. Open **Thonny** from the Start menu. The interpreter shown at the bottom right should be local Python 3. If you see MicroPython, click the interpreter name and choose **Local Python 3** or Thonny’s bundled Python.
3. Choose **File → Open** and select the extracted `main.py`. The upper editor pane is where you write your program. The **Shell** below shows messages when it runs. Choose **View → Shell** if it is hidden.
4. Press **F5** (the green **Run current script** button). Look for `Welcome to Charting Champions!` in the Shell.

## Check that you can draw charts

At the `>>>` prompt in the Shell, type `from pygal import Bar` and press Enter. If a fresh prompt appears, you are ready.

![Thonny Shell shows the welcome message, followed by the Pygal import and a fresh prompt.](img/checkpoint-setup.png)

If you see `ModuleNotFoundError`, open **Tools → Manage packages**, search for **pygal**, select the package named **pygal** and click **Install**. Close the package window and try the import again. If installation is restricted, ask your facilitator to add Pygal to the selected interpreter.

For the next step, click back into the **main.py editor tab**. Save your changes with **Ctrl+S** and run them with **F5**.

los.title: Create your first chart
los.contentMd:
# Create your first chart

Replace the starter code in `main.py` with:

```python
from pygal import Bar

chart = Bar()
chart.title = 'Olympic medals - historical teaching sample'

us = ['United States', 2399]
chart.add(us[0], us[1])

chart.render_to_file('chart.svg')
```

With the `main.py` tab selected in Thonny, press **F5**. In File Explorer, open the extracted folder and double-click `chart.svg`. If prompted, choose a web browser. Keep the chart open. After each edit, run the script in Thonny and refresh the browser tab.

`Bar` is a chart type imported from a library. A library is reusable code written by other programmers. `chart.add()` adds a labelled series, and `render_to_file()` creates the picture.

## Checkpoint

Your chart has one bar, labelled United States, with a value of 2399. Change the title to include your initials and run the code again.

![One bar for the United States reaches 2399 on the medal scale, shown before adding your initials.](img/checkpoint-first-chart.png)

These values come from the original project's historical teaching example. Do not describe them as the latest Olympic totals.

los.title: Store data in lists
los.contentMd:
# Store data in lists

Look at this line:

```python
us = ['United States', 2399]
```

A list groups related values inside square brackets. Python counts positions from zero:

| Expression | Value | Type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `us[0]` | `'United States'` | Text/string |
| `us[1]` | `2399` | Whole number/integer |

Add these lists and chart entries **before** the final `render_to_file()` line:

```python
ru = ['Russia', 1413]
gb = ['Great Britain', 1304]
chart.add(ru[0], ru[1])
chart.add(gb[0], gb[1])
```

Run the code and refresh the chart. Predict what would happen if you tried `gb[2]`. That position does not exist: it causes an `IndexError`.

## Read a chart

![Three bars compare the United States, Great Britain and France.](img/short_list.png)

The original project shows a different selection of three teams. Match each bar to its team using the legend. Which two teams appear in both this picture and your chart?

## Your turn

Add France with 780 medals and Germany with 671 medals. Create one list and one `chart.add()` call for each. Keep the output line last.

## Checkpoint

There are five bars. The United States bar is the tallest in this sample. Explain to your partner why `chart.add(gb[0], gb[1])` needs both indexes.

![Five medal bars in descending order: United States, Russia, Great Britain, France and Germany.](img/checkpoint-five-teams.png)

If chart interactivity loads, hover over a bar and click a name in the legend. What changes when you hide the largest series? If hover is unavailable, read the scale and labels instead.

los.title: Read data from a file
los.contentMd:
# Read data from a file

Typing a list for every country would take a long time. A CSV file stores values in rows with commas between columns.

![Five numbered CSV rows, each with a team name and medal count separated by a comma.](img/csv_sample.png)

Look at the first row of this source example. Which character separates the name from the count? The numbers down the left are editor line numbers. Your file uses a different historical sample.

In Thonny, choose **File → Open** and select `medals.csv` from your extracted folder. Choose **All files** in the file picker if needed. It contains the same five historical sample rows and no heading row:

```text
United States,2399
Russia,1413
Great Britain,1304
France,780
Germany,671
```

Click the `main.py` tab. Choose **File → Save as** and save it as `lists_chart.py` in the same folder. Reopen `main.py` using **File → Open** so your list version stays available. In `main.py`, replace the lists and `chart.add()` calls with:

```python
with open('medals.csv', encoding='utf-8') as data_file:
    for line in data_file:
        print(line.strip())
```

Leave the import, chart creation and output line in place. Run it. An empty chart is expected at this stage: you have printed the file contents but have not added them to the chart.

`with open(...)` opens the file and closes it when the block finishes. The `for` loop visits each row. Four spaces indent each nested level. `strip()` removes surrounding whitespace, including the newline at the end of a row.

## Checkpoint

![Thonny Shell prints the five rows from medals.csv, starting with United States,2399 and ending with Germany,671.](img/checkpoint-csv-shell.png)

Thonny’s Shell displays five rows. Explain which line repeats and why. If Python cannot find the file, run the program from the extracted starter folder.

los.title: Turn file rows into bars
los.contentMd:
# Turn file rows into bars

Each line read from a file is text. Split it at the comma and convert the second item into a number.

In Thonny, replace the contents of `main.py` with this program. Press **F5**, then refresh the browser tab showing `chart.svg`.

```python
from pygal import Bar

chart = Bar()
chart.title = 'Olympic medals - historical teaching sample'

with open('medals.csv', encoding='utf-8') as data_file:
    for line in data_file:
        if line.strip():
            pieces = line.strip().split(',')
            team = pieces[0]
            medals = int(pieces[1])
            chart.add(team, medals)

chart.render_to_file('chart.svg')
```

The `if` skips blank lines. `split(',')` makes a two-item list. `int()` changes text such as `'2399'` into the number `2399`. The output line is outside the loop, so the completed chart is saved once.

This simple parser is for our two-column examples without quoted commas. Real CSV files can be more complicated; Python's `csv` module handles those cases.

## Checkpoint

The file-driven chart matches your five-bar chart. You no longer need a separate `chart.add()` line per country.

![Reading medals.csv produces the same five bars, from United States at 2399 to Germany at 671.](img/checkpoint-five-teams.png)

## Try a change

Make a copy named `practice.csv`, add `Example Team,100`, then change the filename in your program. Update the title to say "Practice data". You should now see six bars. The additional team is fictional.

los.title: Investigate population and wealth
los.contentMd:
# Investigate population and wealth

The original project asks whether population and GDP might help explain medal counts. A chart can suggest a question, but cannot prove its explanation.

## First, practise with fictional data

The starter ZIP includes three files for the same three **invented countries**. None of these values describes a real country.

| File | Values | Conversion | Suggested title |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `practice_medals.csv` | Medal count | `int()` | Fictional medals |
| `pop.csv` | Population in millions | `float()` | Fictional population (millions) |
| `gdp.csv` | GDP in billions of example currency units | `float()` | Fictional GDP (billions) |

1. Save your medal program before editing it.
2. Change the input filename to `practice_medals.csv` and update the title. Change the output filename to `practice-medals.svg`, then press **F5**.
3. Repeat for `pop.csv`, using `population = float(pieces[1])` and `chart.add(team, population)`. Save as `population.svg`.
4. Repeat for `gdp.csv`, using `gdp = float(pieces[1])` and `chart.add(team, gdp)`. Save as `gdp.svg`.

Use `float()` because population and GDP examples contain decimal values. Preserve a separate output for each chart so you can compare them.

## Discuss

- Does the country with the most people have the most medals in this fictional example?
- Does the country with the largest GDP have the most medals?
- Why can we not use invented data to make claims about real countries?
- What other information might matter: years participating, sporting investment, or events entered?

## Original-project extension

Open [Charting champions](https://projects.raspberrypi.org/en/projects/charting-champions/0) and use its supplied medal, population and GDP files to repeat the investigation with its historical datasets. Keep those files in a separate folder so they do not get mixed with our fictional examples. Check dates, units, coverage and country definitions. If those details are unavailable, state that limitation. Do not assume historical medal totals and a population snapshot cover the same period.

## Checkpoint

Show three correctly titled charts and describe one pattern and one limitation. Association is not proof that one factor caused another.

Compare each browser tab with its example below. Check the title and the scale on the left.

**practice-medals.svg**

![Fictional medals. Exampleland has 12 medals, Sample Isles 20 and Demovia 8.](img/checkpoint-fictional-medals.png)

**population.svg**

![Fictional population in millions. Exampleland has 5.2, Sample Isles 1.8 and Demovia 12.4.](img/checkpoint-population.png)

**gdp.svg**

![Fictional GDP in billions. Exampleland has 150.5, Sample Isles 80.2 and Demovia 320.8.](img/checkpoint-gdp.png)

los.title: Make it your own
los.contentMd:
# Make it your own

Choose one extension:

## Try a pie chart

Change both `from pygal import Bar` to `from pygal import Pie` and `chart = Bar()` to `chart = Pie()`. Keep the rest of the program. A pie chart shows parts of the data included; our five-country sample is not a complete world medal total.

## Chart a class survey

Create `survey.csv` with anonymous counts, for example:

```text
Football,8
Surfing,5
Cycling,6
Other,4
```

These are example counts. Replace them with your class's totals, without collecting names. Load the file and give your chart an accurate title. Compare bar and pie charts: which makes the differences easier to see?

## Explain your work

Show a partner your chart and explain the list indexes, loop and number conversion. Save your Python and CSV files together.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: pygal` | In Thonny, select local Python 3 and install pygal via **Tools → Manage packages**. |
| `NameError` for `Bar` | Use capital `B` and import `Bar`. |
| `FileNotFoundError` | Run from the folder containing the named CSV file. |
| `IndexError` | Every nonblank row needs two comma-separated values; indexes are 0 and 1. |
| `ValueError` | Remove heading rows and thousands separators; use `float()` for decimals. |
| `IndentationError` | Use four spaces per level; do not mix tabs and spaces. |
| Empty or outdated chart | Add data before rendering, rerun the program, then refresh the SVG. |
| No hover or legend interaction | The browser/network may block the chart script; use the static chart and labels. |

## Finished?

You should have a list-based chart, a CSV-based chart, and an explanation of what the data means. Optional [worked solutions](archives/charting-champions-solutions.zip) are available after you have tried the tasks.

Text and images adapted from [Charting champions](https://projects.raspberrypi.org/en/projects/charting-champions/0), [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). The school-visit edition uses Thonny, local SVG files and a shorter medal dataset. Full creator credit is in the course README.
